Civic literacy · 2026 general electionNovember 3, 2026 · checked as of

A new architecture of American leadership

Not left versus right. Top versus bottom.

In November 2026, voters propelled an unprecedented cohort of barrier-breaking leaders into statehouses, the Senate, Congress, and City Halls. This interactive intelligence grid transforms election outcomes into an accessible civic education tool.

The 2026 midterms swept Democrats into power in states Trump carried easily, including Kansas, Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Ohio. The winners ran as pastors, loggers, pediatricians and teachers against corruption, billionaire money, the price of gas and groceries, and Big Tech’s data centers. This is the who, the why and the how, with the evidence and the places where the story is less tidy than it sounds.

01 · The scale

The Senate and governor counts above were rechecked on November 19; every Senate and governor race has been called, though no count is certified yet. The House popular-vote margin and the other figures are as of their sources’ dates. Four House races were still undecided on November 19 (see below).

Since election night · updated November 19

  • Alaska Senate, November 17. Democrat Mary Peltola beat Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, 50.1% to 45.8%, enough to win outright in the first round of Alaska’s ranked-choice count; the margin is about 12,500 votes. It was the last Senate race called. Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats (54 Democrats and two independents who vote with them) to 44 Republicans, after nine flips. The count is uncertified (Alaska Beacon, Ballotpedia, Wikipedia). Read the Peltola profile.
  • Governors, November 13. Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won Alaska, the last governor’s race called. Democrats will hold 30 governorships to Republicans’ 20, up from 24. They flipped Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas. Kansas, uncalled on November 6, stayed Democratic: Cindy Holscher led 50.3% to 49.7% (StockAnalysis, Wikipedia).
  • House, still counting. Democrats won the majority on election night. In Wikipedia’s running tally on November 19 they had won 258 of 435 seats and Republicans 173, with four races undecided; Yahoo News said the final majority could reach 260. On November 18 Democrats nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York for speaker (Wikipedia, Yahoo News).
  • Mississippi Senate, November 11. Democrat Scott Colom beat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, 49.2% to 48.7%, a lead of about 4,700 votes. AP called it on uncertified results and Hyde-Smith conceded. Democrats then had 55 Senate seats; the Alaska call on November 17 made it 56 (NPR, ABC News). Read the Colom profile.
  • Hegseth impeachment, November 10. The House voted 211 to 204 to send Rep. Thomas Massie’s impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, which ends the effort for this Congress. Eleven House Democrats and seven Republicans did not vote (States Newsroom). This was the House, not the Senate. Who the absent Democrats are and who backed them.
  • Senate Democratic leader, November 12. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced he will run for Senate majority leader against Chuck Schumer. Schumer says he has the votes; Van Hollen called himself the underdog. Democrats vote by secret ballot in December (NPR, Roll Call, CNN).

Rechecked on November 19: the Senate, governor and seat counts, the items above, and the vote shares for all 29 profiled winners. Everything else on the site is as of its stated date.

02 · Who moved

The coalition, group by group

Compared with Trump’s 2024 vote, Republican House candidates lost ground with nearly every group. The biggest swings came from Hispanic voters, independents and the young. The smallest came from white voters without a college degree, the core of the Republican base, which matters for how far “even conservatives” really goes.

Republican share of the vote by group. Source: Brookings, Nov. 6, 2026.

03 · Why

Six forces beneath the wave

None of these is a culture-war issue. Each is about money, power or basic needs: what things cost, who gets rich from government, who controls the platforms and the power grid, whether you can see a doctor, and whether anyone checks the people at the top.

04 · How

The winning playbook

Across very different states and ideologies, the winners repeated a handful of moves. Read these as patterns in the coverage, not a proven formula.

    Analytical synthesis

    Three structural insights

    Patterns that show up across races, each with the evidence for it and the limits of what that evidence can show.

    Context

    The wave in numbers

    Democrats won the Senate 56 to 44 (54 Democrats plus two independents who vote with them), 30 of the 50 governorships, and a House majority. Every Senate and governor race has now been called; four House races were still undecided on November 19. Nine Senate seats flipped: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. All but Maine are in states Trump carried in 2024. Counts are unofficial until certified.

    Sources: Wikipedia (Senate), Wikipedia (governors), StockAnalysis, Alaska Beacon, Ballotpedia, Al Jazeera/AP.

    Municipal power matrix

    Who actually runs your city

    Most of the roughly 11,000 U.S. municipalities with 2,500 or more residents use one of two structures. Which one your city uses decides whether the mayor you elect runs anything, and who answers when a service fails.

    Compare the two structures

    Forms of government

    Share of 10,969 municipalities with 2,500+ residents, ICMA 2018.

    Claims about efficiency

    The often-repeated line that council-manager cities are “nearly 10% more efficient” comes from a 2011 IBM benchmarking study of 100 large cities, not peer-reviewed research. ICMA reports that 66% of Moody’s Aaa-rated cities had a professional manager in 2016. Both are associations: well-off, stable cities may simply be more likely to choose professional management.

    $61,723

    Average pay for a full-time mayor (ICMA 2018).

    $9,286

    Average pay for a part-time mayor. Low pay narrows who can afford to serve.

    27.2%

    Share of city council seats held by women (ICMA 2018). 32% of cities elect some or all of their council by district.

    Mayors of the 100 largest cities

    Ballotpedia, November 2026. At the start of 2026, 81% of the top-100 population lived under a Democratic mayor; 22 of these seats were on the 2026 ballot.

    What the 2026 mayoral results show

    Term limits drove much of the turnover. In Chandler, Irving, Knox County and Boca Raton the incumbent could not run, so the seat changed hands without any voter rejecting a sitting mayor. A change in a mayor’s party is not always a change in voters’ minds.

    Many mayoral races are officially nonpartisan. Party labels do not appear on the ballot in Chandler, Irving or Los Angeles, so descriptions such as “Democratic gain” rely on candidates’ registrations or endorsements, which are not always public.

    Defeating an incumbent is rare. Los Angeles was the exception: Karen Bass became the first sitting mayor there to lose since 2005, after the Palisades Fire and rising homelessness. Most incumbents on this list who ran were re-elected comfortably.

    The calendar is local. Florida cities often vote in March, Wisconsin in April, Texas in May and North Dakota in June. A common mistake is to assume every result came from November 3: this year’s mayoral races above were decided in March, April, June and August as well.

      The shadow government

      Nearly 40,000 special districts

      A special district is a separate local government created for one job: fire protection, water, sewers, libraries, hospitals, mosquito control. Many can levy property taxes and issue bonds, and each has its own board. The Census Bureau counted 39,555 in 2022, and 40,199 in its 2025 update, out of roughly 91,000 local governments. The commonly quoted “38,000” is the 2017 count.

      The tax stack over one home

      Illustrative rates

      One address can sit inside a county, a city, a school district and several special districts, each taxing separately. The rates here are hypothetical and chosen only to show the structure; look up your own on your county assessor’s tax bill.

      Annual tax

      Taxing boards

      Elected seats

      Ask yourself: how many of these boards’ members could you name? How many of their elections did you vote in?

      What special districts do

      Census Bureau function counts, 2022, grouped by this site. Total 39,555.

      Case study · Missoula County, Montana · February 2026

      On February 10, county commissioners declared 12 special-district boards elected by acclamation because every candidate was unopposed, among them the Missoula Irrigation District. They cancelled elections in 15 more, including the Missoula Rural Fire District and the Turah Meadows Sewer and Water District, because nobody filed at all; those seats were opened for appointment. Local coverage shows the same thing happened in 2018, 2021, 2022 and 2025. It is routine, which is the point.

      Missoula County release →

      When only landowners vote

      Some water districts limit voting to landowners, weighted by acreage. The Supreme Court upheld this in Salyer Land Co. v. Tulare Lake Basin (1973) and Ball v. James (1981), reasoning that these districts serve land rather than people. It is one of the few places in American government where one person, one vote does not apply.

        Campaign capital

        Follow the money

        The 2026 midterms are projected to be the most expensive on record, and a small number of very large donors supplied much of the outside money. This is the money side of the “top versus bottom” story: how much was spent, who paid, what the biggest races show, and how to check the money where you live. Every figure has a date and a source. Where outlets disagree, we show the range.

        In one minute

        What this page shows

        1. The 2026 midterms are projected to cost $11.9 billion, the most expensive on record (OpenSecrets).

          Go to: How much →

        2. A few very large donors supply much of the money: 515 donors who each gave at least $1 million put $4.2 billion into super PACs, more than 70% of all the money super PACs raised.

          Go to: Top donors →

        3. The top 100 donors’ share of all federal election spending was 1.5% in 2008, before the 2010 Citizens United ruling, and has been 14–16% since 2016.

          Go to: How we got here →

        4. The referee is missing: the Federal Election Commission has lacked a quorum for most of this cycle (Brennan Center, Oct. 13). With two of its six seats filled, it cannot investigate or impose penalties.

          Go to: The rules →

        5. Money does not always win. In the four 2026 races on this page (the Texas Senate race, Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, and the Georgia and Ohio governor’s races), the side that spent more lost.

          Go to: The biggest races →

        6. Payments from foreign governments to Trump businesses and Kushner’s firm are documented. We found no court, inspector general or jury finding that a payment caused a decision.

          Go to: Gulf money analysis →

        7. AIPAC and its super PAC are the largest country-focused election spenders we found. In what we could check, no public evidence shows Israel directs or funds AIPAC. Whether it should have to register is argued on both sides.

        How much

        $11.9B

        Projected total federal election spending in 2026, up from $8.9 billion in 2022 (about $10.2 billion adjusted for inflation). OpenSecrets projection, reported Nov. 4, 2026.

        $3.9B

        Projected spending by outside groups on 2026 federal races, up 85% from four years earlier. OpenSecrets, Oct. 30, 2026. It counts what outside groups spend and leaves out money passed between committees.

        $1.47B+

        “Dark money,” gifts from donors who are not named, flowing to outside groups. A lower bound and a record; 2024’s total was $1.35 billion. OpenSecrets.

        515

        donors who each gave at least $1 million put $4.2 billion into super PACs by late October, more than 70% of all the money super PACs raised this cycle. Public Citizen, Oct. 27, 2026. This counts money super PACs received. The $3.9 billion counts money outside groups spend. Super PACs pass money to one another and keep cash in reserve, so the money raised can be larger than the money spent.

        ~$2B

        from just the 20 biggest donors to federal races, through the mid-October filing deadline. New York Times ranking, reported Nov. 1, 2026.

        $737M

        in corporate political spending through Oct. 23, up 60% from the 2024 presidential cycle and more than four times 2022. Public Citizen.

        How we got here

        Since the 2010 Citizens United ruling, the biggest donors have moved from the edge of campaign money to its center

        On January 21, 2010, the Supreme Court’s Citizens United v. FEC decision removed restrictions on independent spending by corporations and unions. Outside spending, which candidates do not control, has grown from $574 million in 2008 to close to $4.5 billion in 2024, and most of it is spent by super PACs.

        Outside spending in presidential-election cycles, in millions of dollars. OpenSecrets, published Jan. 24, 2025. The 2012 and 2024 figures are reported as “nearly $1.3 billion” and “close to $4.5 billion.”

        1.5% → 14–16%

        The top 100 individual donors’ share of all federal election spending: 1.5% in 2008 ($80.9 million of $5.3 billion), and between 14% and 16% since 2016. OpenSecrets, Jan. 24, 2025.

        $2.6B

        spent in 2024 by billionaire donors and their families, nearly 20% of all federal election spending, over 80% of it through channels not allowed before 2010. It has multiplied by a factor of 163 since the ruling. Roosevelt Institute report, Oct. 2025, citing Americans for Tax Fairness.

        $290M+

        from one billionaire to outside spending groups in 2024, about the combined gifts of 3 million small donors. OpenSecrets data, as cited in the Roosevelt Institute fact sheet.

        Read more: dark money, what Americans think, and what research says (3 paragraphs)Show less

        Dark money has grown the same way. Nonprofits that do not name their donors spent $1.2 million on federal elections in 2006 and $257 million in 2012 (OpenSecrets data, via Common Cause, Jan. 2015). The Brennan Center counted more than $1.9 billion across the 2024 federal races, up from about $1 billion in 2020, and at least $4.3 billion since 2010. It says that is probably a substantial undercount. The 2006 to 2012 numbers and the 2020 and 2024 numbers measure different things.

        Most Americans see the problem. In Pew Research Center surveys from mid-2023, 80% said big campaign donors have too much influence on what members of Congress do, 70% said people in their own district have too little influence, and 72% supported limits on how much individuals and organizations can spend on campaigns. Brennan Center polling from June 2, 2026, cited in its October article, found that nine in ten voters say government prioritizing billionaires and large corporations is corrupt, and that majorities in both parties blame campaign donations.

        Researchers disagree about what the ruling did. An NBER working paper (July 2023, not peer-reviewed) compared the 23 states that had banned independent political spending with states that had not. After the ruling it found total income about 2% higher and labor income up to 3% higher in the states that had had bans, more turnover among governors and legislators in both parties, less polarized legislatures, and fewer state enforcement actions against labor and consumer-protection violations. The authors read this as more political competition. The Roosevelt Institute fact sheet cites other state-level studies of the same kind of states (we did not read them) that found corporate tax rates cut by 4 to 8 percent and Republican candidates’ success rates up 4 to 11 percentage points. Both are studies of state governments.

        What the biggest races show

        Texas Senate

        $573.2M

        in ad spending in the general election, the most of any non-presidential race in U.S. history (AdImpact, reported Nov. 3, 2026).

        • Outside groups from both parties spent over $205 million on the general election through September, and more than 98% of it supported Republican Ken Paxton (Texas Tribune, Oct. 1).
        • Texas PAC, the group connected to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, spent $131 million. President Trump’s super PAC added nearly $24 million.
        • Democrat James Talarico spent $61 million on ads in the general election (AdImpact).
        • In the primaries, of $49.4 million spent supporting Cornyn, Paxton and Talarico, 36% came from groups that do not disclose donors, and the $13.2 million of dark money backing Cornyn was more than his own campaign raised (Brennan Center, May 2026 roundup, published June 9).

        Result: Talarico won, 55% to 43%, with about 99% of precincts reporting.

        Michigan Senate Democratic primary

        $30.6M

        spent by AIPAC’s United Democracy Project to support Haley Stevens and oppose Abdul El-Sayed, the most it has ever spent on a single race (Sludge, Aug. 3, 2026).

        • In all, more than $60 million went to support Stevens or oppose El-Sayed, against about $3.5 million of outside spending for El-Sayed (Al Jazeera, Aug. 2). About $6.5 million of the $60 million comes from a group that had not reported to the FEC, so that part is from local media.
        • AIPAC’s PAC and super PAC have spent more than $104 million this cycle, the second cycle in a row above $100 million (Sludge).

        Result: El-Sayed won the primary, 49% to 47%, and then the general election.

        Three governors’ races

        Money figures: Brennan Center, “Who’s Trying to Buy the Governor’s Mansion?”, Oct. 27, 2026, drawing on news reports and campaign filings that it did not independently verify. Results are from this site’s checked notes.

        Georgia

        Republican Rick Jackson self-funded over $100 million and outspent Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms “five to one.” Result: Bottoms won, 54.2% to 45.8% with 95% counted.

        Ohio

        Republican Vivek Ramaswamy loaned his campaign at least $36 million, and Jeff Yass gave at least $30 million to a super PAC backing him. He and allied groups spent over $120 million on ads, more than triple the spending for Democrat Amy Acton. Result: Acton won, 52.3% to 44.4% with 97.7% counted.

        Wisconsin

        Three megadonors (Diane Hendricks and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein) accounted for 92% of Republican Tom Tiffany’s fundraising in the three months before the report. State law limits labor union PACs to $86,000 for Democrat David Crowley. Result: Crowley won, about 54% to 45%, and Tiffany conceded.

        In Texas, Michigan, Georgia and Ohio, the side that spent more lost. Four races do not prove that money never wins. They show that it does not always win. Before the election, The Washington Post reported that Republicans’ roughly half-billion dollars of spending since the summer did not appear to have moved the polls, as the Brennan Center notes.

        The rules changed, and the referee is missing

        More money is moving through fewer limits, with little enforcement

        • Independent expenditures by super PACs and other groups hit a record $2 billion through the end of September, up 51% from the last midterm cycle after inflation.
        • In June the Supreme Court struck down limits on how much party committees can spend in coordination with their candidates (National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC). The Senate GOP spent $48 million in coordination with its candidates through August, the bulk of the $63 million spent this way by all four congressional party committees. The NRSC’s spending alone is three times what all four committees spent in coordination by the end of August 2022.
        • Party-affiliated super PACs have increased their spending tenfold since 2014. Together they spent $494 million through September, including $280 million from two Senate Republican-linked groups, SLF PAC and Texas PAC.
        • The Federal Election Commission has lacked a quorum for most of this cycle. With only two of its six seats filled, it cannot investigate, impose penalties or make new rules.

        Brennan Center, Ian Vandewalker, “Big Money Breaks Records, Boosts GOP,” Oct. 13, 2026. Independent expenditures run through September; coordinated spending through August.

        The other side of the ledger

        Small donors are giving, in huge numbers

        $586M

        raised from small-dollar donors for Democratic candidates, causes and organizations in the second quarter of 2026. The average gift was $39. ActBlue, July 9, 2026.

        15M

        contributions in that one quarter, including 573,000 from first-time donors. It was ActBlue’s best non-presidential quarter on record.

        Compare the scale: it took 15 million small gifts in one quarter to raise $586 million, while 515 donors gave $4.2 billion to super PACs over the cycle so far. These are different measures. ActBlue is one platform, on the Democratic side, for one quarter, and the figure comes from its own release. The super PAC number covers the whole cycle so far.

        What people are doing about it

        Voters in three states moved to limit big money

        On November 3, 2026, Montana voters approved Initiative 194, “the Montana Plan,” with about 65% of the vote (Daily Montanan, Nov. 4). It would bar corporations, nonprofits and other organizations from spending money to support or oppose candidates, parties or ballot measures. Individuals acting on their own and political committees are exempt (NBC Montana, Nov. 6).

        It is not settled. It takes effect on January 1, 2027 unless a court blocks it. A federal lawsuit filed on election night by the Frontier Institute, the Montana Republican State Central Committee and other groups argues it violates their First Amendment rights and asks a court to pause it.

        Michigan. Voters approved Proposal 2 on November 3 with about 81% yes, 3,550,297 to 805,646 with most precincts counted (ClickOnDetroit, Nov. 4). It bars regulated utilities such as DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, and government contractors with more than $250,000 in state contracts, along with people associated with them, from making campaign contributions (WXYZ). The Mackinac Center for Public Policy sued in federal court on November 3, arguing the measure violates the First Amendment because it would require journalists, nonprofits and others to file reports when they speak about elected officials.

        Alaska. In the August 18 primary, voters approved a measure reinstating limits on individual campaign contributions, by roughly 3 to 1 in early results (Alaska Public Media) and by more than 70% according to the Brennan Center. It sets $2,000 per candidate per two-year cycle for individuals and $4,000 for political groups, adjusted for inflation once a decade, and takes effect after the November general election. Alaska has had no individual limit since a federal appeals court struck down its $500-a-year limit in 2021.

        Read more: other reforms proposedShow less

        Other reforms on the table. The Brennan Center’s policy agenda (Jan. 20, 2026) proposes four changes to campaign money: amend the Constitution to restore campaign finance limits, ban big donations from government contractors, require groups that spend on federal campaigns to disclose their major donors, and publicly fund campaigns. New York already matches small contributions to state candidates at up to $12 to $1. Legislators or voters in 23 states have passed resolutions calling for a constitutional amendment on campaign finance. These are proposals from a think tank, not law.

        Closer to home

        A real example: San Diego City Council, 2022

        Local officials control zoning, building permits, public contracts and labor agreements, so the people affected by those decisions have reasons to fund local campaigns. There is no national database of municipal campaign money, so the honest unit of analysis is one city at a time.

        MapLight / Common Cause California analysis of 2,678 individual donors.

        796 donors who gave the legal maximum, 30% of all donors, supplied about 67% of individual contributions. Real estate and construction interests gave about 17% of council campaign funding. Concentration, not a single industry, is the clearest pattern.

        How to check your own money

        1. For federal races, search donors and committees on FEC.gov, the official record.
        2. For your city or state, find your city clerk’s, county elections office’s or secretary of state’s campaign finance portal.
        3. Download contributions for the races you care about as a spreadsheet.
        4. Sort by employer and occupation. Developers, contractors, and lobbying firms are usually visible.
        5. Look for independent-expenditure committees, which can spend unlimited amounts if they do not coordinate with the candidate.
        6. Compare the money with the votes those officials later cast.

        Analysis · Foreign government money and the presidency

        Gulf money and Trump’s businesses: what the records show, and what they do not

        The question

        Did money from foreign governments to businesses tied to the president produce policy decisions?

        The short answer

        The payments are documented. We found no court finding, inspector general report, indictment, plea or jury verdict that says any decision was made because of a payment.

        This is an analysis block, not a news item. Each claim below is labelled by who made it. Open a group to read the claims.

        ✓Documented
        in an official record, court filing or primary document
        ?Alleged
        said by a named person, party or outlet; not established
        ✕Not supported
        the dates or documents cut against it
        ↻Still open
        a lawsuit, review or question not yet settled
        ✎Point of view
        an argument or reading, labelled as such

        Inside the claims, CONFIRMED, REPORTED, CONTESTED and NOT VERIFIED say how each detail was checked.

        ✓DocumentedPayments to Trump properties and Kushner’s firm, the 2019 arms sales and vetoes, the Barrack, Nader and Broidy cases (Barrack acquitted; Nader and Broidy pleaded guilty, and Broidy was later pardoned), and the Saudi nuclear agreement.Show 5Hide
        • Payments to Trump hotels and towers.A January 4, 2024 report by House Oversight Committee Democratic staff, “White House for Sale,” counts at least $7.8 million from at least 20 foreign governments to four Trump properties (the Washington and Las Vegas hotels, Trump Tower and Trump World Tower). The records cover roughly two years of the presidency, and some Saudi and Qatari figures are projected. It is a minority staff report, not a finding of the committee. China is $5,572,548, and at least $5,357,495 of that is an estimate of base rent paid by a Chinese bank for Trump Tower space. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE together are $1,146,391. By our arithmetic, not the report’s, that makes China about 71% of the total and the three Gulf states about 15%. Most of the Saudi figure ($615,422) is an estimate, and so is Qatar’s.
        • Saudi money to Kushner’s firm.Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund committed $2 billion to Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners, with a 1.25% annual fee on the committed funds, according to Affinity’s own disclosure to the Senate Finance Committee (Chairman Wyden’s September 2024 letter). The New York Times reported in April 2022, citing internal fund documents, that the fund’s screening panel objected, citing the inexperience of Affinity’s management and an excessive fee, and that the board, led by the Crown Prince, overruled it days later.
        • Emergency arms sales and vetoes.The administration notified Congress on May 24, 2019 of emergency arms sales worth about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Jordan. Trump vetoed the Yemen war-powers resolution on April 16, 2019 and three resolutions disapproving those sales on July 24, 2019. The Senate did not override either. In August 2020 the State Department’s inspector general found that the Secretary’s emergency certification met the Arms Export Control Act, and also that the Department did not fully assess risks to civilians or put mitigation in place.
        • The Barrack, Nader and Broidy cases.Tom Barrack was indicted in July 2021 on seven counts: acting and conspiring to act as an agent of the UAE without notifying the Attorney General, obstruction and false statements. He was acquitted of all counts on November 4, 2022. George Nader pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States over concealed foreign contributions, reported in January 2022, and was sentenced in July 2023 to a further 20 months after a five-year term on unrelated charges. Elliott Broidy pleaded guilty in October 2020 to conspiracy to violate the Foreign Agents Registration Act over lobbying that included work for the financier Jho Low and the Chinese government, and was pardoned in January 2021.
        • The Saudi nuclear agreement.The United States and Saudi Arabia signed a civil nuclear (Section 123) agreement, completed on July 22, 2026. The White House message sending it to Congress is dated August 24; the Senate record and the House resolution’s title give September 14. A House disapproval resolution (H.J.Res. 217) was introduced on September 16 and a Senate one (S.J.Res. 221) on October 15.
        ?Alleged or attributedClaims by Democrats and in press reports, each with the response: Affinity’s fees, the reasons for the inspector general’s firing, the arms figure, the 2017 nuclear plan.Show 4Hide
        • Affinity’s fees.Senate Democrats estimate “as much as $157 million” from foreign clients over roughly the three years before the September 2024 letter, including $87 million from the Saudi government. A March 2026 letter from Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Robert Garcia estimates $39 million from the Saudi government in 2025 and “more than $110 million” since 2021. The letter says Kushner “may be exploiting certain loopholes” to serve as an unregistered foreign agent. We found no Justice Department or court finding of a violation, and no Affinity response.
        • Inspector general Steve Linick’s firing.Rep. Eliot Engel said the arms-sale review may have been another reason. The State Department denies retaliation and cites management shortcomings, the handling of a leaked report and failure to perform. Trump said he had lost confidence in Linick.
        • Kushner and the arms figure.ABC News, citing anonymous sources, reported that Kushner pushed officials to inflate the “$110 billion” Saudi deal. The New York Times, also from anonymous sources, reported that he advised the Crown Prince after the Khashoggi murder (we read that report only through a relay).
        • The 2017 nuclear plan.House Democratic staff reports in February and July 2019, when Democrats held the committee majority, cited whistleblowers. They allege that White House staff kept working on a plan from IP3, a private company led by retired generals, after National Security Council lawyers warned that legal requirements could not be bypassed. House Republican staff said on July 22, 2019 that the evidence “does not show impropriety.” Barrack sought the Middle East envoy and UAE ambassador posts in 2017 and did not get them; he was named envoy for Syria in 2025. Energy Department authorizations in 2017 to 2019 covered discussions and marketing, and we found no report that a reactor or nuclear material was transferred.
        ✕Not supported by the recordWhere the timing or the documents cut against a payment-for-policy story.Show 4Hide
        • The Qatar blockade came first.The blockade of Qatar began on June 5, 2017. The documented contacts come later: Broidy’s Oval Office meeting on October 6, 2017, a photo of Nader with Trump at a fundraiser on October 25, and another Broidy meeting on December 2. At Barrack’s trial, Treasury Secretary Mnuchin, by then a former secretary testifying for the defense, said Barrack’s position “was clearly in support of Qatar.”
        • Tillerson’s firing.Whether Broidy and Nader caused Secretary of State Tillerson’s firing is contested. The New York Times reported in March 2018 that both urged it, and it does not say that caused it. Trump gave other reasons, mainly the Iran deal.
        • The March 2018 hotel bill and arms notices.The one documented Saudi hotel bill in March 2018, $78,342 for March 7 to 15, came before the Crown Prince’s March 20 visit. About $1 billion in anti-tank missiles was notified on March 22 and reported on March 23, and the $1.3 billion artillery sale was announced on April 5.
        • What the hotel report does and does not say.The Democratic hotel report does not say any payment caused a decision. On the UAE it notes that the stays came while the UAE lobbied on Qatar and asks whether business ties shaped policy. On China it goes further: it notes that Trump did not sanction ICBC, his Trump Tower tenant, and says he put his personal financial interest above the public interest. That is the Democratic staff’s conclusion, not a finding by any court or official body.

        Taken together. So the evidence sits at documented money and requests on one side and documented decisions on the other, with timing in between. Apart from the Democratic staff’s China argument, no source read ties a specific payment to a specific decision. Democrats allege influence; Republicans and Kushner’s lawyers deny it.

        ↻Still openThree open matters: the nuclear review clock, the CREW lawsuit, and Affinity’s new fundraising.Show 3Hide
        • The nuclear review clock.The Saudi nuclear agreement’s 90-day congressional review. The Associated Press reports it ends about December 13, 2026, counting from September 14. Another analysis counts from August 24 and counts only days Congress is in session, so the end date is disputed. Sens. Merkley and Markey say a Senate vote comes after November 29. We found no floor action through November 14.
        • The CREW lawsuit.The watchdog group CREW sued on October 14, 2026 to have Kushner, an unpaid envoy who was not confirmed by the Senate, treated as a government employee. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly called CREW “an unserious, Trump-deranged organization,” and Kushner’s attorney said the suit “is without merit.” Sources differ on whether Kushner is a named defendant. One docket mirror shows the federal defendants’ answer due December 21, 2026 and no ruling as of November 3.
        • Affinity’s new fundraising.The March 2026 letters say Affinity was seeking at least $5 billion more in foreign capital, citing the New York Times, and asked for a response by April 2, 2026. No response was found.

        How this was checked: on November 14, 2026 each claim was tested against original documents where they could be opened (the hotel report, the Senate Finance letters, the State inspector general report, Justice Department releases, the House document sending the agreement to Congress, and the 2019 House reports), and against news reports where they could not. Not opened: the New York Times originals, the Barrack indictment and verdict form, the Nader and Broidy plea agreements, the Mnuchin trial transcript, Defense Department arms-sale notices and congress.gov pages.

        Analysis · Foreign agents law and the Israel lobby

        AIPAC and FARA: what is documented, what is argued, what is not shown

        The question

        Does the record support calling AIPAC a foreign agent working on behalf of Israel?

        The short answer

        Not on the public evidence. AIPAC is a U.S. advocacy organization, not registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), and focused on U.S. policy toward Israel. With its super PAC it is the largest country-focused election spender in the FEC data we read. No public evidence shows Israel directs or funds it.

        This is an analysis block, not a news item. It tests a common claim: that AIPAC is a U.S. organization, not registered as a foreign agent, whose sole goal is to influence U.S. legislation, elections and military policy on behalf of Israel.

        What the law asks. The Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) requires registration when someone acts at the order, request, direction or control of a foreign government or foreign political party. A foreign principal is a foreign government or party, or a person or entity outside the United States. So the legal question turns on who directs the organization, not on how large or focused it is.

        Labels: CONFIRMED means a primary document or two independent outlets; REPORTED means one outlet or an attributed claim; CONTESTED means sources disagree; NOT VERIFIED means we found no adequate source.

        ✓Documented
        in an official record, court filing or primary document
        ?Alleged
        said by a named person, party or outlet; not established
        ✕Not supported
        the dates or documents cut against it
        ↻Still open
        a lawsuit, review or question not yet settled
        ✎Point of view
        an argument or reading, labelled as such

        Inside the claims, CONFIRMED, REPORTED, CONTESTED and NOT VERIFIED say how each detail was checked.

        ✓DocumentedWhat AIPAC is, what it says about itself, how FARA’s lobbying exemption works, its election spending, its October 2026 change, and congressional travel.Show 6Hide
        • What AIPAC is.AIPAC is a U.S. nonprofit organized under section 501(c)(4) of the tax code. Its revenue was $156.4 million in fiscal 2024 and $122.5 million in fiscal 2025 (ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer, from its tax filings). CONFIRMED.
        • What AIPAC says about itself.Its stated aim is to persuade the U.S. government to adopt policies supporting the U.S.-Israel relationship. It says it is funded exclusively by Americans and is neither funded nor directed by the Israeli government. That is AIPAC’s own description. No audit confirms the funding claim, and its tax filings do not list donors.
        • The lobbying exemption.FARA’s exemption for registered lobbyists under the Lobbying Disclosure Act does not apply where a foreign government or foreign political party is the principal beneficiary, according to the Justice Department’s own FAQ. AIPAC’s lobbying registration would therefore not shield it if an agency relationship with Israel were shown. It would not prove one either. CONFIRMED.
        • Election spending.AIPAC’s super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP), is the largest country-focused election spender in the Federal Election Commission data we read, and no other country- or diaspora-focused committee we checked outside the pro-Israel space came near it, including the Pakistani, Hindu, Turkish and Iranian American PACs (none reported independent expenditures) and the Indian-American Impact Fund ($2.8 million in 2024). The totals disagree by source. For 2024, the FEC’s own figure for UDP’s independent expenditures is $37.9 million (total disbursements $61.4 million), and The Intercept gives $41.4 million. For 2026 the reported figures run from $53.6 million (FEC, through August 31) to $66.7 million (The Intercept) because the cutoff dates differ. The largest non-Israel committee we found, a pro-Palestinian super PAC called American Priorities, had about $7.9 million in independent expenditures in 2026 through October 14.
        • The October 2026 change.On October 21, 2026, AIPAC announced it would end endorsements, direct PAC contributions and earmarked giving, and shift to organized contributions from individuals. UDP continues. “AIPAC has a PAC” is no longer an accurate description of its direct giving. CONFIRMED (NPR).
        • Congressional travel.A POLITICO and Howard Center database found Israel was the top destination for privately sponsored congressional trips, and about 75% of the Israel trips were sponsored by AIPAC’s affiliated foundation, the American Israel Education Foundation. The database covers House trips only. REPORTED.
        ⇄Argued, both sidesWho says AIPAC should register, who says the law does not require it, and the dual-loyalty dispute.Show 3Hide
        • Registration.Rep. Thomas Massie introduced a bill on May 14, 2026 that would let a U.S.-organized group be covered if objective indicia show a foreign country is a principal beneficiary of its lobbying, even without direct foreign funding or instruction. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee; we found no later action. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said on August 7, 2025 that AIPAC should register as a foreign lobbyist. She did not name FARA. REPORTED.
        • The other side.FARA lawyer Matthew Sanderson, who does not represent AIPAC, told the Forward that the law is clear AIPAC need not register, because regulators look at foreign funding, contracts and control, not shared interests. Sen. Ted Cruz said on June 18, 2025 that Israel does not direct AIPAC. REPORTED. Massie’s bill suggests its sponsor thinks current law does not reach AIPAC. That is our inference, not something he is reported to have said.
        • Dual loyalty.The Anti-Defamation League calls the dual-loyalty charge an age-old antisemitic trope. Some Jewish writers disagree: M.J. Rosenberg wrote that AIPAC should register, and the American Council for Judaism republished it and says registration deserves serious consideration. Both views are published. Neither is evidence about who funds or directs AIPAC.
        ✕Not supported by the recordFour parts of the common claim that the record does not support as stated, and a 1962 precedent.Show 5Hide
        • “On behalf of Israel” is CONTESTED.No source we read shows Israeli direction, control or funding of AIPAC, and AIPAC denies both. The single-issue focus is real, so “sole goal” holds as to scope. Scope does not establish agency.
        • “No other nation has this set-up” fails as stated.Other diaspora groups also run advocacy nonprofits and PACs, and several governments register more FARA-reported spending than Israel. OpenSecrets’ Foreign Lobby Watch puts Israel tenth for 2016 to 2025, at about $212 million, behind China, Japan, Liberia, Saudi Arabia, the Marshall Islands, South Korea, the Bahamas, Qatar and the UAE. Those totals include tourism and trade promotion, and about $83 million of Israel’s came from its government. The narrower claim holds: AIPAC and UDP dwarf every other country-focused election committee we found, and Israel leads privately sponsored congressional travel. Whether that is a difference in scale or in kind is a values question the record does not settle.
        • “Foreign interference by another name” is a characterization, not a finding.The documented Israeli-government influence work of 2024 to 2026 ran through other channels, and no source we read links it to AIPAC. Contracts routed through the Havas agency, such as Clock Tower X (FARA registration 7649, registered September 18, 2025), are on the public FARA register. Absence from the sources we read is not proof that nothing exists, and we did not search the registry’s lists of persons contacted.
        • “Many say AIPAC should register” has no current poll behind it.We found no 2024 to 2026 poll that asked. The polls we found measure favorability. In an April 2026 Echelon Insights poll, 18% were favorable and 25% unfavorable. “And those it funds” is not supported by any source we read.
        • Past precedent.In November 1962 the Justice Department ordered AIPAC’s predecessor, the American Zionist Council, to register, citing funds from the Jewish Agency, according to records archived by the advocacy group IRmep. We found no government-hosted original. Foreign funding triggered the order, not shared goals, and it did not involve AIPAC itself.

        The narrower wording the evidence supports: AIPAC is a U.S.-incorporated advocacy organization, American-funded by its own account, and not registered under FARA. Its stated and documented focus is U.S. policy toward Israel. With UDP it has been the largest country-focused election spender in the FEC data we read, and its affiliate sponsors most of the privately funded congressional trips to Israel. No public evidence shows Israel directs or funds AIPAC. Some members of Congress and advocacy groups argue it should register, a 2026 House bill would change the law to allow that, and FARA lawyers quoted in the press say current law does not require it.

        How this was checked: the claims were drawn from a research report and then tested against original documents where they could be opened (the Justice Department’s FARA text and FAQ, the FEC and FARA registries, ProPublica, AIPAC’s own statements, the NPR and Forward reporting). Items we could not open are labelled. AIPAC does not appear in the FARA registry’s list of active registrants. We did not search the list of terminated registrations or the status of other diaspora groups.

        Where the numbers disagree, and what we could not confirm
        • Elon Musk’s total. Reports range from $366 million (New York Times, via the Brennan Center, Oct. 13) to $445 million (Public Citizen, Oct. 27), $446 million (Al Jazeera, Oct. 27) and $483 million for Musk and his company (Brennan Center, Oct. 29, data through Oct. 14). The difference is the cutoff date and what is counted.
        • Texas Senate. $432 million is all spending in the primaries and general election through September (Texas Tribune). $573.2 million is ad spending alone in the general election (AdImpact). They measure different things.
        • Dark money has two counts. OpenSecrets’ $1.47 billion (so far in 2026) and $1.35 billion (2024) count gifts to outside spending groups. The Brennan Center’s $1.9 billion for 2024 also counts direct spending and TV and online ads, so it is a wider measure, and the Brennan Center calls it an undercount.
        • Totals still moving. OpenSecrets’ $11.9 billion is a projection until all reports are filed. Dark money and corporate totals will rise as late reports come in.
        • Donor lists differ a little. Al Jazeera and Public Citizen both use FEC data but count differently. For example, they give the Uihlein family $150 million and $146 million.
        • Not found. A single total for billionaires’ giving, and the share of 2026 money from donors giving under $200. OpenSecrets figures are from its own Oct. 30 projection, read on opensecrets.org.

          Law & courts

          The justice ecosystem

          Most people meet the justice system locally: a sheriff’s deputy, a prosecutor, a judge, a county jail. In much of the country, voters choose the people who lead those offices, often in races with only one name on the ballot. This page shows who holds which power, the numbers behind it, what happened at the polls in 2026, and what you can look up and ask where you live. Every figure has a date and a source.

          In one minute

          What this page shows

          1. Nearly 2 million people are confined in more than 6,000 places, at a cost of at least $445 billion a year.

            Go to: The scale →

          2. Prosecutors are elected in 45 states, but only 23% of their elections from 2020 to 2024 were contested.

            Go to: Prosecutors →

          3. Trials are rare: in fiscal 2018 about 90% of federal defendants pleaded guilty and about 2% went to trial (Pew, 2019).

            Go to: Pleas and trials →

          4. 1,412 agreements let local agencies do immigration enforcement with ICE (287(g)), as of February 13, 2026.

            Go to: Immigration →

          5. State supreme court races cost a record $157.3 million in 2023–24, and outside groups outspent the candidates for the first time.

            Go to: Cost of the bench →

          6. About 4 million Americans could not vote in 2024 because of a felony conviction. Most people held in jail before trial keep the right to vote.

            Go to: Voting →

          7. Epstein: officials and courts documented a 2007 deal that kept him out of federal court, and serious failures at the jail where he died. Allegations against named people are unproven, and each response is shown.
