          The shape of it

          Nearly 2 million people are confined, in more than 6,000 places

          ~2M

          people confined in prisons, jails, immigration detention, juvenile facilities and other places. Prison Policy Initiative, Mar. 11, 2026.

          $445B

          a year, at least, is what the whole system costs: about $417 billion in government spending and about $28 billion paid by people in the system and their families (Prison Policy Initiative, Following the Money of Mass Incarceration 2026).

          465,000

          people are held before trial, 426,000 of them in local jails. About 120,000 more are in jail after a conviction, generally for misdemeanors with sentences under a year.

          +58%

          growth in ICE detention between 2025 and 2026, about 25,200 more people. The report says immigration detention accounts for virtually all of the growth in mass incarceration since its last report.

          $54.3B

          spent by governments on immigration policing and detention in 2025, up from $20 billion in 2017 (about $26 billion in today’s dollars). That is 13% of the $417 billion governments spend on the criminal legal system.

          12% · 15%

          Local jails hold about 12% fewer people, and state prisons about 15% fewer, than in 2019.

          Number of facilities by type, 2026 (Prison Policy Initiative). The report also counts military prisons, civil commitment centers, psychiatric facilities and prisons in the territories.

          What to take from this. Local jails are the most numerous kind of facility, 3,116 of them, and most sheriffs’ offices run one. The fastest growth is in immigration detention, which is federal. That is why who runs your county jail, and what agreements they sign, matters.

          Who holds the power

          Four offices decide most of what happens to a person

          OfficeHow the person gets the jobWhat the office decidesWhat the numbers show
          SheriffTypically elected, county by countyRuns the jail in most counties, courthouse security, patrol and serving papers2,900 sheriffs’ offices were 20% of general-purpose police agencies but employed 25% of their sworn officers; about 10% of sheriffs’ sworn officers were assigned to jail duties (BJS, Dec. 31, 2020)
          Prosecutor (district attorney)Elected in 45 statesWhether to charge, what to charge, plea offers, bail requests and diversion programsOnly 23% of 3,231 prosecutor elections from 2020 to 2024 were contested (UNC, May 13, 2026)
          JudgeSome form of election in 39 states; appointed in othersBail, trials, sentences and what the law meansTrial judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections in 21 states and partisan elections in 11 (Brennan Center, updated Apr. 2023)
          Public defenderFunded and organized by counties or states, or contracted outDefends people who cannot afford a lawyerPennsylvania was one of only two states that did not fund public defense for decades (Spotlight PA, Apr. 1, 2026)

          Sheriff

          Gets the job: typically elected, county by county.

          Decides: runs the jail in most counties, courthouse security, patrol and serving papers.

          The numbers: 2,900 sheriffs’ offices were 20% of general-purpose police agencies but employed 25% of their sworn officers; about 10% of sheriffs’ sworn officers were assigned to jail duties (BJS, Dec. 31, 2020).

          Prosecutor (district attorney)

          Gets the job: elected in 45 states.

          Decides: whether to charge, what to charge, plea offers, bail requests and diversion programs.

          The numbers: only 23% of 3,231 prosecutor elections from 2020 to 2024 were contested (UNC, May 13, 2026).

          Judge

          Gets the job: some form of election in 39 states; appointed in others.

          Decides: bail, trials, sentences and what the law means.

          The numbers: trial judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections in 21 states and partisan elections in 11 (Brennan Center, updated Apr. 2023).

          Public defender

          Gets the job: funded and organized by counties or states, or contracted out.

          Decides: defends people who cannot afford a lawyer.

          The numbers: Pennsylvania was one of only two states that did not fund public defense for decades (Spotlight PA, Apr. 1, 2026).

          County sheriff

          Elected

          • — Covers the whole county
          • — Usually runs the county jail
          • — Patrols unincorporated areas
          • — Serves warrants and court orders
          • — Answers to voters

          City police chief

          Appointed

          • — Covers one city
          • — Usually no long-term jail
          • — Enforces state and city law
          • — Hired by the mayor or manager
          • — Can be removed by them

          Prosecutors

          The most powerful office most people never choose between candidates for

          Local prosecutor elections were held in 45 states from 2020 to 2024. Of 3,231 regular elections, 23% were contested. Voters had less choice than in any period the researchers have studied.

          Share of local prosecutor elections that were contested. Prosecutors and Politics Project, Carolina Law, May 13, 2026.

          In 2026, all 15 of Oregon’s district attorney races have one candidate. Bolts found it is the only cycle this century in which that is true. Five of the 12 incumbents first got the job by a governor’s appointment, not an election. Lawyers and advocates told Bolts that harsh campaigns, fear of career damage and low pay keep challengers out.

          Trials are rare

          Most cases end in a plea

          2% · 90%

          of about 80,000 federal defendants in fiscal 2018, about 2% went to trial and about 90% pleaded guilty. About 8% had their cases dismissed (Pew Research Center, 2019).

          State data are patchier. In 2017, jury trials were fewer than 3% of criminal cases in the 22 jurisdictions with data, including 0.86% in Texas and 2.91% in New York (National Center for State Courts, via Pew). Critics argue that defendants who go to trial and lose can face much higher sentences than those who plead. That claim comes from a 2018 defense lawyers’ report, not from Pew’s data.

          What to take from this. If trials are rare, most outcomes are set earlier, by what a prosecutor charges and what plea they offer. That is why a contested prosecutor race is often the only moment voters can weigh in on those choices.

          Sheriffs, jails and immigration

          Many sheriffs now act as immigration enforcement partners

          1,412

          active 287(g) agreements between ICE and local agencies as of Feb. 13, 2026, across 40 states and territories. NPR, Feb. 17, 2026.

          1,130+

          agreements signed in 2025 alone, compared with just 45 signed in 2019, during President Trump’s first term (NPR).

          234 of 254

          Texas counties, by a bill author’s count, are covered by a state law that requires counties running a jail to join the program. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2026, with compliance required by Dec. 1, 2026 (WJLA, July 2025).

          Read more: how 287(g) works and how states differ (2 paragraphs)Show less

          A 287(g) agreement lets local officers do some immigration enforcement. There are three models. Under the jail model, everyone booked into a local jail is checked for legal status. Under the warrant model, local officers serve administrative warrants on people already in the jail. Under the task force model, officers can stop, question and arrest people for immigration violations, with ICE supervisor approval. ICE reimburses participating agencies for the salary and benefits of each trained officer, and for overtime up to 25% of salary.

          States differ. Florida’s governor has effectively required local agencies to sign. Virginia’s governor ordered state agency agreements ended. Critics, including a University of California, Irvine law professor, warn of racial profiling and costly lawsuits, and the Government Accountability Office has said the program needs better oversight. The Department of Homeland Security calls the profiling allegations “categorically false,” and a Heritage Foundation analyst calls the concerns overblown.

          What to take from this. A sheriff’s choice about 287(g) is made locally, and in some states it is required by law. Whether your county has an agreement, under which model, is a public fact you can ask about.

          Sheriffs: money and accountability

          Elected sheriffs answer to voters, and have to raise money to win

          What to take from this. Between elections, a sheriff may face few formal checks. Researchers are measuring how elections shape what sheriffs do, and one large county has written a rule for removing one. Campaign finance reports for a sheriff’s race are usually public, though the Common Cause researchers said getting records from some sheriffs’ offices was hard.

          Read the evidence: campaign money, election years, “constitutional sheriffs,” a removal rule (4 parts)Show less
          • Who pays for sheriff campaigns. A Common Cause report with Communities for Sheriff Accountability (December 2021) examined campaign finance records of sheriffs in 11 states, covering less than 3% of sheriffs’ offices. It counted about 13,000 apparent conflicts of interest, mostly between 2010 and 2021. It treated gifts from jail-related businesses, and from companies that might do business with a sheriff’s office, such as construction, food service and health care, as potential conflicts. About $6 million, roughly 40% of the $15.7 million it examined, fell in that category. In Bristol County, Massachusetts, the jail’s health care contractor spent more than $20,365 on Massachusetts sheriffs’ campaigns, $12,040 of it for the county’s sheriff, and the state’s sheriffs paid it $9.82 million in contracts from 2012 to 2021. The authors did not judge whether any gift was illegal, chose sheriffs by a mix of public interest and random selection, and are advocacy groups.
          • Election years change behavior. A study of 57 California counties from 2003 to 2020 (Su and Buerger, American Journal of Political Science, 2024) found traffic-fine revenue fell 30% in sheriff election years, and only in the election year. The drop was larger when the incumbent ran again or the race was highly contested. The authors expected sheriffs to ease enforcement to avoid voter anger, and did not test that motive directly. It is one state.
          • Sheriffs who answer only to voters. A 2025 Georgetown Law Journal article by Vanderbilt law professor Farhang Heydari describes “constitutional sheriffs” as sheriffs who view themselves as the highest authority in their county, answerable only to their electorate. They have declared opposition to gun control measures, pandemic restrictions and environmental protections, among other things. He notes that other sheriffs have declared opposition to immigration and abortion restrictions, so it is not one-sided. He argues that courts should again decide when a sheriff’s refusal to enforce a law amounts to neglect of duty, as state courts once did.
          • A county that wrote a removal rule. In November 2022, Los Angeles County voters approved Measure A, a charter amendment that lets the Board of Supervisors remove a sheriff by a four-fifths vote. The grounds include violating a law related to the sheriff’s duties, flagrant or repeated neglect of duty, misusing public funds, falsifying an official document, and obstructing an investigation. The sheriff gets written notice and a chance to be heard first. The county’s Sheriff Civilian Oversight Commission had urged the Board to put it on the ballot.

          Before trial

          Jails and bail

          Most people in a local jail on a given day have not been convicted. Since 1997, all of the net growth in jails has come from people held before trial (Prison Policy Initiative).

          One state’s experiment. Illinois became the first state to end cash bail on September 18, 2023. In the first year, Loyola University researchers found jail populations fell, but far less than predicted. The share of people who missed court dates went from about 17% to about 15%. They found no documented rise in crime comparing the first six months of 2023 with the first six months of 2024, and said plainly: “We can’t say whether it’s had an impact on crime.” The findings were preliminary.

          What to take from this. A few years of data from one state can tell you what did not happen. It cannot settle what caused it, and honest researchers say so.

          The right to a lawyer

          The promise is national. The funding is local.

          In 1963 the Supreme Court held that a poor person’s trial cannot be fair unless a lawyer is provided. Estimates say between one-third and one-half of people who qualify are represented by assigned or contract lawyers, according to the Vera Institute (Feb. 17, 2026), which says public defense has been funded at “drastically lower levels” than prosecution and police for decades.

          Read more: a close look at PennsylvaniaShow less

          A close look at Pennsylvania. Counties are still the main funders. The state began giving $7.5 million a year in 2023, spread across 67 counties. A committee found the state about 400 lawyers short for adult criminal cases, and nearly 40% of lawyers hired in the past five years have left. In up to 20% of cases, court records showed no representation or “unknown” representation, though the data may be incomplete. The ACLU of Pennsylvania sued in 2024, and the case is ongoing (Spotlight PA, Apr. 1, 2026).

          Courts

          How states choose supreme court justices

          Initial selection method, all 50 states (Ballotpedia). Kansas voters rejected a switch to elections on August 4, 2026.

          Assisted appointment (often called the Missouri Plan): a commission screens candidates, the governor picks one, and the judge later faces a yes-or-no retention vote.

          Retention elections are a later step, not a separate method, so a chart that counts them as a method alongside elections double-counts states.

          2026 results

          State supreme court elections

          • Texas. Democratic challengers defeated all four Republican justices seeking reelection to the Texas Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice. Republicans still hold a 5–4 majority. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals now has a 6–3 Republican majority.
          • Ohio. Democrats gained a seat on the Ohio Supreme Court. Republicans keep a 5–2 majority.
          • North Carolina. Justice Anita Earls won reelection. Republicans keep a 5–2 majority. The race drew over $8 million, on track to be the most expensive state supreme court election of the year.
          • Montana. Amy Eddy won. A citizens’ initiative to put nonpartisan judicial elections into the state constitution passed with 68%.

          Brennan Center State Court Report, Nov. 4, 2026 (updated Nov. 5). The authors say the results are not likely to immediately change any state high court majorities, and set up fights for majorities in 2028. Money is a factor in these races: Wisconsin’s 2025 Supreme Court race drew about $57 million in outside spending (Brennan Center, as cited by the Roosevelt Institute).

          The cost of the bench

          State supreme court races are the most expensive ever

          $157.3M

          spent on state supreme court races in the 2023–24 cycle by candidates, interest groups and parties. That is 35% more than 2019–20 and almost twice 2015–16, adjusted for inflation. Brennan Center, Feb. 26, 2026.

          $85M · $70M

          Interest groups spent $85 million (54%) and candidates $70 million (45%). It was the first time outside groups outspent the candidates.

          30%

          of the 119,000 TV ads in these races mentioned abortion rights, up from 3% in 2020. Courts also decide voting rules and district maps, which drew major donors.

          Read more: the biggest races and who paid (2 paragraphs)Show less

          The biggest races: Wisconsin’s 2023 race at $51 million, then the most expensive judicial election in U.S. history; Pennsylvania at $27 million; North Carolina at $10.5 million, a state record; and two Montana races at $6.8 million and $5.9 million.

          The money came from both sides. Groups on the left supplied 64% of interest-group spending: groups backing liberal candidates spent $55 million and conservative-backed groups $30 million. The report names dark money groups on both sides, among them A Better Wisconsin Together and WMC in Wisconsin. Fair Courts America disclosed that $9 million of its $12 million came from Richard Uihlein, while some groups reveal donors only in tax filings long after the election.

          What to take from this. When a court decides abortion, voting rules or district maps, who sits on it becomes worth spending on. Voters in states that elect judges are the ones who see that money in their ads.

          Police and accountability

          What the data say, and what the law allows

          1,314

          people killed by police in 2025, down 5% from 1,383 in 2024. It is the first decrease in six years. Mapping Police Violence, Feb. 2026.

          3.6

          people a day, on average. The group warns that federal agencies are expanding use of force and some states are rolling back reforms such as limits on vehicle pursuits.

          Qualified immunity. On March 23, 2026, in Zorn v. Linton, the Supreme Court held that a Vermont sergeant who used a wristlock on a protester at a sit-in was protected from a lawsuit, because no earlier case with similar facts clearly said his conduct was unconstitutional. Courts, the decision says, generally need to point to such a case. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, dissented.

          Mapping Police Violence counts publicized killings from news reports and official sources. Other outlets cite slightly lower 2025 totals.

          Safety

          What is happening to crime

          −51%

          Homicides in 30 large cities in the first half of 2026 were 51% below the 2022 peak, 18% below the first half of 2025 and 31% below the first half of 2019.

          ~4.0

          per 100,000: the 2025 national homicide rate, an estimate that would be the lowest since at least 1900 if FBI data confirm it.

          Carjacking fell 47% in the first half of 2026, the largest drop of 13 offenses. Drug offenses rose 12%, the largest rise. The Council on Criminal Justice says there is “no single or easy explanation,” that the report is not evidence for or against any policy, and that the cities studied may not represent the nation (July 23, 2026).

          Who is affected, and who can vote

          The justice system also decides who gets a voice

          ~4M

          Americans were denied the right to vote because of a felony conviction in the 2024 federal election. The Sentencing Project, Oct. 29, 2026.

          1 in 22

          voting-age Black Americans is blocked from the ballot, more than three times the rate of non-Black Americans.

          56%+

          of Virginia voters approved an amendment on Nov. 3, 2026 that restores voting rights automatically when people leave prison. Before, they had to petition the governor.

          Maine, Vermont and Washington, D.C. let citizens vote while incarcerated. In 2026, Missouri restored voting rights to more than 41,000 people on felony probation and parole, and a federal court ruling sharply narrowed Virginia’s policy. The Virginia count is early reporting, not the certified result.

          Who is imprisoned. The Sentencing Project’s 2021 report, using 2019 federal data, found Black Americans were imprisoned at nearly five times the rate of white Americans, and one in 81 Black adults was in state prison. That report is old, so treat the exact ratio as an estimate. The direction is the point.

          The jail voting gap

          About 78% of people held in U.S. jails in 2024 had not been convicted of the charge they were held on (Prison Policy Initiative, using federal data). Most pretrial detainees keep the right to vote, and the sheriff running their jail, the prosecutor and sometimes the judge may all be on their ballot.

          There is no national figure for how many actually vote. A court-ordered Massachusetts report released in June 2026 found 1% turnout among eligible people in jail in the 2024 primary and 5% in the general election. Harris County, Texas opened the state’s first jail polling place in November 2021.

          “Unconvicted” and “eligible” are not the same: some detainees are ineligible for other reasons.

          Jail voting that worked

          When a jail runs a polling place, people vote

          25%

          of people held in Cook County Jail (Chicago) voted in the June 2022 primary: 1,384 of 5,560. That beat the 20% turnout of registered voters in the city, and about half of them used same-day registration. Prison Policy Initiative, Oct. 25, 2022.

          <7%

          In the same jail’s 2018 primary, before in-person voting, only 394 people voted, by absentee ballot. In the 2020 general election, more than 2,000 of about 5,400 did, roughly 37%.

          13

          of an estimated 26 eligible people voted at the Harris County Jail in Texas in the March 2022 primary. In the first election there, in November 2021, 96 did.

          Read more: why it is hard, where it exists, and the law (3 paragraphs)Show less

          Why it is hard. The average jail stay is about 28 days, too short for a mail ballot to go out and come back. Jail is not a recognized reason for an absentee ballot in several states. Many people do not know they can vote or think their charge disqualifies them. Photo ID can be confiscated at intake, as in Texas, and registration forms and stamps can be hard to get. Cook County officials estimate 80% of people in their jail are eligible to vote (Center for Public Integrity, Sept. 15, 2022).

          Where it exists. Jail polling places have run in Cook and Will counties in Illinois, Washington, D.C., Denver, Harris County in Texas and Los Angeles County (Prison Policy Initiative, 2022).

          The law. In 1969, in McDonald v. Board of Election Commissioners, the Supreme Court framed a jailed voter’s claim as a right to receive absentee ballots and noted nothing in the record showed they were absolutely barred from voting. In 1974, in O’Brien v. Skinner, it struck down a New York law that let some jailed people vote absentee but not people held in their home county, calling the exclusion “wholly arbitrary” for people awaiting trial or serving misdemeanor sentences who had no other way to vote.

          What to take from this. Most people held before trial keep the right to vote. Whether they can use it depends on whether the jail and the county elections office make it possible, and both are run locally.

          What voters decided in 2026

          A record of the year, so far

          • August 4, Kansas: voters rejected a switch to electing supreme court justices.
          • November 3, Virginia: voters approved automatic voting rights restoration after prison, with more than 56% in early reporting.
          • November 3, Montana: 68% voted to put nonpartisan judicial elections in the constitution.
          • November 3, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina: the supreme court races above, with Democrats gaining seats in Texas and Ohio and Republican majorities holding.
          • All year, Oregon: all 15 district attorney races had one candidate.

          We found no national tally of 2026 district attorney or sheriff results, so this list covers what we could confirm.

          Look it up, then ask

          Build your own picture of your county

          Look up

          • Who is on your ballot, from sheriff to judge: Ballotpedia’s sample ballot lookup.
          • How often your state’s prosecutor races are contested: the Prosecutors and Politics Project.
          • How many people your county jails and sends to prison, over time: Vera’s Incarceration Trends.
          • Your state’s numbers and profile: Prison Policy Initiative state profiles.

          Ask candidates

          A sheriff

          Does your office have a 287(g) agreement, and under which model? How many people in your jail are held before trial, and for how long? Who investigates when someone dies in custody?

          A district attorney

          Will you publish data on charges, plea offers, dismissals and diversion? How do you decide when to ask for bail?

          A judge or judicial candidate

          How do you weigh pretrial release? Who funds your campaign?

          Analysis · Elite impunity and the Epstein record

          The Epstein record: what officials have found, what is alleged, what is not shown

          The question

          Does the public record show the powerful getting outcomes ordinary defendants would not, and is that a divide between top and bottom rather than left and right?

          The short answer

          Officials and courts have documented a 2007 deal that kept Epstein out of federal court, victims kept in the dark about it, and serious failures at the jail where he died. Allegations against named people are unproven, and each person’s response is shown. On releasing the files, votes crossed party lines; on who is to blame, they split by party.

          This is an analysis block, not a news item. Official findings are kept apart from allegations, and every allegation sits beside the response of the person named. Where a death is mentioned, we give what the official findings say.

          ✓Documented
          in an official record, court filing or primary document
          ?Alleged
          said by a named person, party or outlet; not established
          ✕Not supported
          the dates or documents cut against it
          ↻Still open
          a lawsuit, review or question not yet settled
          ✎Point of view
          an argument or reading, labelled as such

          Inside the claims, CONFIRMED, REPORTED, CONTESTED and NOT VERIFIED say how each detail was checked.

          ✓Documented by officials or courtsThe 2007 deal and 2008 plea, the ethics review, the jail failures, the files law, Congress’s findings on banks, the 2025 memo.Show 6Hide
          • The 2007 agreement and 2008 plea.Jeffrey Epstein avoided federal charges under a non-prosecution agreement signed in September 2007 and pleaded guilty in state court in June 2008 to solicitation of prostitution and procuring a minor for prostitution. He was sentenced to 18 months and served under 13, with work release. Victims were not told of the agreement until July 2008, about ten months after it was signed, and the 11th Circuit said they were left in the dark. The full court later ruled, over four dissents, that the victims’ rights law gives no private right to sue outside an existing proceeding, so with no charge filed they could not enforce their rights.
          • The Justice Department’s ethics review.In November 2020 its Office of Professional Responsibility found that then-U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta showed “poor judgment” but committed no professional misconduct. Victims’ lawyers and Sen. Tim Kaine objected.
          • The jail.The Justice Department’s Inspector General reported in June 2023 that guards missed required checks and counts and falsified records, that about half of the cameras were not recording after a July 29, 2019 disk failure, and that Epstein was taken off suicide watch on July 24. Two guards entered deferred prosecution agreements in May 2021 and a judge dismissed the charges in January 2022. The medical examiner ruled suicide, and the Inspector General found nothing contradicting the FBI’s finding that no crime was involved. A pathologist hired by Epstein’s brother said the evidence leaned toward homicide, short of a final conclusion. Where reporting questions the manner of death, it is opinion, and the official findings show no crime.
          • The transparency law.The House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act 427 to 1 on November 18, 2025, the Senate acted by unanimous consent, and it became law on November 19. The Justice Department missed the December 19 deadline and posted more than 3 million additional pages, nearly 3.5 million in all, on January 30, 2026. How much remains withheld is disputed: Rep. Massie said in July that more than 3 million files remain (reported), Rep. Garcia said on November 10 that more than 2.5 million pages do, and we found no Justice Department figure after January 30.
          • Congress on the banks and agencies.The House Oversight Committee’s Republican majority report of November 10, 2026 says the government failed survivors for decades, that crimes after 2005 could have been prevented, and that financial institutions missed warning signs. It recommends a Treasury review. The Justice Department said the recommendations had already been addressed.
          • The 2025 memo.A July 7, 2025 Justice Department and FBI memo concluded suicide, found no client list and cited no credible evidence of blackmail. A minute of jail video was missing from the first release. A fuller version later released by Congress includes it, and CBS reports that it contradicts Attorney General Bondi’s explanation that the system resets nightly. Provenance questions remain.
          ?Alleged or contested, with the responseUnproven allegations involving Trump, Blanche, Black, Staley, Groff, Lutnick, Levine, Fekkai and others, each beside the person’s response or denial.Show 12Hide
          • Trump and Blanche.House Judiciary Committee Democrats (ranking member Raskin) released a report on October 26, 2026 (a staff report, page 52) that 11 women tie Trump to Epstein’s operation, five of whom accuse him directly. Its press release says Trump and Paolo Zampolli “may have been co-conspirators,” and the report says Trump abused women alongside Epstein. It also says Todd Blanche, now Attorney General and then Deputy Attorney General, may have engaged in obstruction and potential witness tampering in his July 2025 interview with Ghislaine Maxwell, and it calls for a special counsel. The Oversight Republicans’ November 10 report says it identified no documents implicating Trump. A White House spokeswoman told Spectrum News none of the allegations are true, and a Justice Department spokesperson reportedly called the report a last-ditch effort to mislead the public. The allegations are unproven, and the dispute runs along party lines.
          • Leon Black.He stopped answering questions in a June 26, 2026 interview and did not appear for a subpoenaed September 3 deposition. The Oversight Committee voted unanimously, both parties, to hold him in contempt on September 15, and the House approved it September 16 without a formal vote. A 2021 review commissioned by Apollo found he paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, which the review and Sen. Wyden describe as payment for tax and estate-planning services; Wyden puts the total at $170 million. We saw no charge against him. He sued the committee on September 3. His lawyers say he knew nothing of Epstein’s conduct and call the action politically motivated.
          • Jes Staley, Lesley Groff and others.Staley told the committee he had no specific recollection of emails in question, and denies wrongdoing. Groff, Epstein’s former secretary, was interviewed June 9, 2026 and denies knowing of abuse. The majority report calls Staley’s claimed lack of recall not credible and says DOJ should further investigate Groff. Their accounts are reported, not findings.
          • Philip Levine and Frédéric Fekkai.Sarah Kellen told the committee on May 21, 2026 that Levine, the former Miami Beach mayor, and Fekkai, the hairstylist, assaulted her. Comer referred Levine to DOJ on June 4. Levine’s spokesperson described a brief encounter with another consenting adult about 25 years ago, and other reports say he denies the allegation. Fekkai’s representative calls it categorically false. Neither has been charged.
          • Les Wexner.The Oversight report faults Les Wexner for giving Epstein control of his foundation and power of attorney; Wexner told the committee he was conned. Reported, not a finding of wrongdoing.
          • Bill Clinton.Bill Clinton was deposed on February 27, 2026 and said he had no knowledge of the abuse. Reported, not a finding of wrongdoing.
          • Jean-Luc Brunel.Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was arrested in December 2020 and found hanging in a Paris jail in February 2022; one report says the inquiry concluded suicide.
          • Gérald Marie.Gérald Marie’s lawyer denies accusations in new Paris complaints.
          • Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor.Britain’s Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on February 19, 2026 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and released under investigation; on October 8 a court agreed the search warrants were unlawful, and he denies wrongdoing.
          • Simon Andriesz.Simon Andriesz, a whistleblower, was found dead outside Bangkok on September 23, 2026; his family says suicide and no foul play, and we found no source linking his death to his disclosures.
          • Daniel Siad.Daniel Siad, a scout named in the files, was found dead at his home near Paris on July 20, 2026, with the cause pending an autopsy.
          • Howard Lutnick.He told a Senate hearing in February 2026 that he visited Epstein’s island with his family in 2012. Members of both parties, including Reps. Massie and Khanna, called for his resignation in February, and in May every Democrat on the House Oversight Committee demanded it. We found no finding of wrongdoing.
          ✎Analysis: the site owner’s reading, tested“Top versus bottom” tested: what supports the reading, and what cuts against it.Show the testHide

          The owner’s reading is that this is not a contest of right against left but of the powerful against everyone else. This is editorial analysis, not a verified finding. The record supports part of it:

          ✓What supports it

          • Votes crossed party lines.The votes crossed party lines. The 2025 vote was 427 to 1, the lone no being Rep. Clay Higgins (R-La.). The 2025 discharge petition to force a vote was led by Massie, with Republicans Greene, Boebert and Mace also signing, and the 2026 petition for a second bill reached the 218 signatures needed on November 11, 2026, with Republicans Massie, Mace, Norman and Fitzpatrick signing. No House vote on it has occurred. The Black contempt vote was unanimous in committee, and a Republican chairman, James Comer, introduced a bill on survivors’ nondisclosure agreements.
          • Polling.A Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1,117 adults on February 13 to 16, 2026 (margin of error 3 points) found 69% said the Epstein files show powerful people are rarely held accountable, answering extremely or very well. By party: Democrats 81%, independents 68%, Republicans 58%. A majority in every group agrees, with a 23-point gap between the parties. We read only headlines of the other polls on the subject, so those are NOT VERIFIED.

          ✕What cuts against it, or cannot test it

          • The timing of the 427-to-1 vote.The 427-to-1 vote came two days after Trump urged a yes vote on November 16, 2025, so it shows near-unanimity once opposing leadership gave way. The 2026 petition drew only four Republicans. Massie lost his May 19, 2026 primary to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein; Roll Call says his disputes with Trump included the Epstein records, but we found no source saying the Epstein dispute caused the loss.
          • Who forced the votes.The people who forced the votes were members of Congress. The pattern is rank-and-file members against leadership and the executive. That is not the same as the public against the elite.
          • Blame splits by party.On who is to blame, and on Trump in particular, the record is partisan: the two House reports reach opposite conclusions, and Democrats and Republicans give different figures for what is still withheld.
          • No proven enterprise, no proven election effect.We found no evidence of a single coordinated enterprise, and none that Epstein caused any 2026 election result. AP called Colorado’s 4th District on November 13 for Eileen Laubacher over Rep. Lauren Boebert, who reportedly conceded. Boebert signed the 2025 petition and did not sign the 2026 one. No source we read gives a cause.

          Where that leaves it. The narrower statement the evidence supports: on whether the powerful escape accountability and whether the files should be released, the votes and headlines cross party lines; on who is to blame, they do not. The Ipsos result fits the view that the belief is broadly shared across parties, though not equally. Whether “top versus bottom” is how the public divides cannot be tested with one poll.

          How this was checked: the claims were drawn from a research report and then tested against original documents where they could be opened (the Inspector General’s report, court opinions, House and Senate releases, roll-call records, Justice Department statements). Some primary documents could not be opened in full, including both House reports’ full text; those items rest on the committees’ releases and press accounts. Allegations are shown with the named person’s response.

          Where the numbers disagree, and what we could not confirm
          • Police killings. Mapping Police Violence counts 1,314 for 2025. Other outlets cite about 1,200. The difference is how and when deaths are counted.
          • Racial disparity. The Sentencing Project’s five-to-one figure is from 2019 data and a 2021 report. A Prison Policy Initiative page appears to give a higher ratio, about six to one; we saw that only in a search summary and did not read it.
          • Illinois bail. The Loyola findings are from the first year and are preliminary. Later reports by advocacy groups and think tanks reach different conclusions, and we did not read them in full.
          • 287(g) agreements. The count rose through 2026. NPR’s 1,412 is as of Feb. 13. Later counts we saw in search results came from sources we did not read.
          • Judges. The count of states that elect judges is from a 2023 update. We did not find 2026 results for Michigan or Washington supreme court races, or Wisconsin’s April 2026 race.
          • Sheriff campaign money. The Common Cause report is by advocacy groups, covers a small share of sheriffs’ offices, defines “conflict” broadly, and did not test whether any gift was illegal or changed any decision.
          • Election-year traffic fines. One state, California, from 2003 to 2020. The motive is the authors’ expectation, not a tested result.
          • Jail voting. Turnout figures are county and advocate counts. There is no national figure. We read McDonald only as the later O’Brien opinion quotes it. For Los Angeles County’s Measure A we confirmed that it led by a wide margin on election night, but did not open a source with the final percentage.
          • Not found. A national tally of 2026 district attorney and sheriff elections, the number of people in state prisons from the 2026 report we read, and a national count of public defender shortages. A researcher told Stateline the national picture is “a complete black box.”
          Sources for this section

            Interactive electoral mechanics

            Ranked choice, round by round

            In ranked choice voting (also called instant runoff), you rank candidates. If no one has more than half of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots move to each voter’s next choice still in the race. That repeats until someone has a majority of the ballots still counting. Washington, D.C. used it for the first time in June 2026.

            2026 at the ballot box

            • 16 jurisdictions used it in 2026, including Alaska, Maine, NYC and San Francisco.
            • Longmont, CO adopted it with about 56%.
            • Irvine, CA measure leading, not yet called.
            • Honolulu rejected it: 44.6% yes among votes cast on the question.
            • Alaska repeal losing on election night with about 52% no; absentee ballots count for 15 days.

            1. Shape the electorate

            Each bloc is a group of voters who cast the same ranking. Drag a slider to change a bloc’s size, or change its rankings. Leave a choice blank to model voters who rank fewer candidates. Total:

            Candidates are fictional. Ties for last place are broken by ballot order; real jurisdictions use lot or other statutory rules.

                  Languages

                  How translation works

                  This site is written in English, and English is the original. When you choose Español or العربية, your browser translates the page on your device where it can. Chrome and Edge on desktop do this from the language buttons. Firefox, Safari and phone browsers have their own Translate feature, which the language buttons explain.

                  The site sends no text anywhere to be translated. Translations can contain errors, so the English original is the authoritative version. Names, quotations and legal designations are left as written, and charts are not translated.

                  How power is built

                  Three writers, one shared question: who does the work?

                  Most guides tell you what to do. These three books explain why some efforts last and others fade after one campaign. They are arguments by their authors, not settled findings, and each one is labeled that way below.

                  Jane McAlevey

                  No Shortcuts: Organizing for Power in the New Gilded Age (Oxford University Press, 2016). She separates three methods. Advocacy is experts working for people. Mobilizing is calling the same committed supporters to the next event. Organizing is building a majority of ordinary people who lead their own fight. She argues the first two can win a vote but rarely change who holds power.

                  Source: publisher and reviews (Labor Notes, Commons Library). She died July 7, 2024.

                  Hahrie Han

                  How Organizations Develop Activists (Oxford University Press, 2014). She argues that groups that first build depth, meaning people who take on real roles, can later reach breadth by mobilizing many more. Her field experiments, published in the American Political Science Review in 2016, found that asking people inside a relationship raised petition signing, recruiting others and meeting attendance.

                  Source: Oxford University Press; APSR (2016). Her claims are research findings from specific groups, not rules for every setting.

                  Mark and Paul Engler

                  This Is an Uprising (Nation Books, 2016). They contrast momentum-driven organizing, which uses sudden public moments to draw in new people, with structure-based organizing, which builds lasting membership. They argue that movements need both.

                  Source: publisher description and reviews.

                  What to take from this. Before joining or starting something, ask whether it is asking you to attend an event or to take a role other people depend on. McAlevey, Han and the Englers disagree on details, but all three treat that difference as the one that matters.

                  Read more: terms and limits (2 paragraphs)Show less

                  McAlevey uses two terms worth knowing. An organic leader is someone whom coworkers or neighbors already follow, whether or not they hold a title. A structure test is a task that shows whether a campaign really has a majority behind it, such as getting most coworkers to sign a petition or show up. Her critique of Saul Alinsky’s style of community organizing appears in a Labor Notes review of her work, so treat it as her argument as reported by a reviewer.

                  Not used here because it could not be confirmed: a three-part scheme attributed to Han in the research notes we were given, a claim about a specific union local’s results, and a credit for the “Movement Ecology” framework. The page leaves them out rather than guess.

                  The path to office

                  Most elections Ballotpedia tracks have one name on the ballot

                  Ballotpedia tracks every congressional, state executive, state judicial and state legislative race, plus local races in the 100 largest cities, every state capital and 475 school districts. In 2025, 68% of the 38,609 elections it tracked in 49 states were uncontested (26,318). In 2024 the share was 70% (53,485 of 76,902). Ballotpedia says its totals likely undercount the problem, because canceled elections and seats where nobody filed are hard to count.

                  Share with no major-party competition, 2024. Ballotpedia.

                  The measures differ. The 38% counts state legislative seats with no major-party opponent (2,227 of 5,807). The 70% counts elections with one candidate on the ballot. The 78% is 2,845 law-enforcement elections.

                  How many offices?

                  Ballotpedia puts it above 500,000

                  Ballotpedia says there are more than 500,000 elected offices, with no as-of date. We found no current official count, and no source for the common “96% are local” figure. Treat “the large majority are local” as the safe version. She Should Run’s own materials use the “500,000+” phrase.

                  Who recruits and trains candidates

                  Five groups, compared

                  • Run for Something recruits and supports candidates aged 40 and under for down-ballot races, and is partisan (progressive). It says it has helped elect more than 1,600 people since 2017, has a pipeline of over 250,000 and, in its own statement, saw 65% of its November 2025 candidates win and 43 seats flip. Its site lists 535 endorsed candidates in 48 states for 2026. We found no published 2026 general-election total.
                  • She Should Run is a nonpartisan 501(c)(3), founded by Erin Loos Cutraro, which became independent in 2011 after starting inside the Women’s Campaign Fund. It aims for 250,000 women running by 2030 and says women take about four years to decide to run. Gifts are tax-deductible.
                  • Emerge trains Democratic women through a six-month program of about 70 hours, and says it has trained over 7,000 since 2002. One news report says it ended its state affiliates in December 2025 in favor of regions. Its own announcement could not be read.
                  • States Win (formerly Sister District) sends volunteers and money into close state legislative races. Its 2024 report names Sister District Project (a 527 political committee) and Sister District Action Network (a 501(c)(4)), so gifts are generally not tax-deductible. How the current States Win, Inc. relates to those entities is not confirmed.
                  • Movement Voter Project moves donor money to local year-round organizing groups. It is partisan and its main arm is a 501(c)(4). The related Movement Voter Fund is a 501(c)(3).

                  What to take from this. “Nonprofit” does not mean the gift is tax-deductible, and “nonpartisan” is each group’s own description. The directory below labels both for every entry. Groups on the right, in the center and across party lines are listed there too, with the same labels.

                  Read more: corrections to figures in circulation (2 paragraphs)Show less

                  A research summary we were given said about 70% of seats lacked competition “in 2020.” Ballotpedia’s 2020 figure is 64% to 65%; 70% is 2024. It also named a different founder for She Should Run and described a student’s 2014 undergraduate capstone (Amy Gooch, Columbia College Chicago) as a journal article. Neither claim is used here.

                  Several phrases attributed to Run for Something, such as a goal of running a candidate for all 500,000+ offices, “nearly 800 elected in 49 states,” and specific demographic percentages, were not found on its site. Its own current figures for elected alumni are about 56% women, 58% people of color and 21% LGBTQIA+. Its tax entities are separate: the Action Fund is a 501(c)(4).

                  Movements and parties

                  Two partisan groups, two different tools

                  Democratic Socialists of America is a membership organization, not a registered party (NPR). On Nov. 3, 2026, six DSA-endorsed candidates won U.S. House races, per NPR citing AP race calls: Avila Chevalier (NY-13), Valdez (NY), Kiros (CO-1), Gonzales-Torres (CA), McKinney (MI) and Rabb (PA). DSA has two House members now, and NPR says that number will grow fourfold when the new Congress is seated in January. DSA says it has more than 120,000 members; City & State reported more than 90,000 dues-paying members in January 2026.

                  Working Families Party is on the ballot in Connecticut, New York and Oregon. The Guardian reported it is active in 18 states in January 2026. Its main tool is fusion voting: a candidate can run on two parties’ lines, so the smaller party can show how many votes it brought.

                  What to take from this. One is a membership organization that endorses candidates. The other can put its own line on the general-election ballot, but only in a few states. Which tool is available depends on where you live.

                  Read more: where fusion voting is allowed (1 paragraph)Show less

                  Fusion voting is fully used only in New York and Connecticut (New America; American Prospect, April 2026). Oregon and Vermont allow candidates to carry more than one party label, but the votes are combined (“dual-labeling”). Counts of WFP candidates and wins in 2026 were not found in a source we could read.

                  Co-governance

                  The word has two meanings

                  Movements sharing power with elected officials

                  Mark and Paul Engler’s A Guide to Co-Governance (2022, Democracy Uprising) describes organized people working inside and outside government after an election win. It lists five practices and five pitfalls, and draws on Brazil’s landless workers’ movement. This is their argument, drawn from case examples.

                  Communities and local governments sharing decisions

                  A second use, described by New America, means residents and local government sharing responsibility for decisions and results, for example through participatory budgeting. Same word, different setting.

                  What to take from this. When someone says “co-governance,” ask which one they mean before you agree or object.

                  Land and energy

                  New high-voltage lines slowed sharply

                  Grid Strategies and the Americans for a Clean Energy Grid report miles of new transmission lines at 345 kV and above. Nearly 4,000 miles were built in 2013. The 2023 figure was first reported as 55 miles and later revised to about 450. The 2024 figure, first reported as 322 miles, was revised to 888 after the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission corrected its data in 2025.

                  Miles of new 345 kV and larger lines. Grid Strategies / ACEG, with revisions of July 23, 2025.

                  Demand

                  Data center demand is projected to rise sharply

                  A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report for the Department of Energy (December 2024) estimated that U.S. data centers used 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, about 4.4% of U.S. electricity. It projected 325 to 580 TWh by 2028, about 6.7% to 12%. These are projections with a wide range.

                  Data center electricity use in terawatt-hours (TWh). DOE, Dec. 20, 2024.

                  What to take from this. A community benefits agreement is a signed contract between a developer and community groups. Three guides to writing one are in the directory: the Center for Community Investment toolkit (2025), the Good Jobs First and Partnership for Working Families handbook, and PowerSwitch Action, which is the new name of Partnership for Working Families.

                  What is not confirmed

                  Left out because we could not verify it

                  • Official certified win counts for 2026 candidates from Run for Something, States Win or the Working Families Party.
                  • Movement Voter Project’s figure for the number of groups it funds and its claimed dollar total for 2026.
                  • A table of land cover by energy type, and a “74 to 132 gigawatt” data center figure. We could not trace either to a source.
                  • One directory page we could not read: the Senate lobbying-disclosure search, which denies access to automated browsers. Its entry is marked Reported in 2026 sources, not Confirmed.
